newsitem.title: LEBANON: World Bank sharply increases funding for Lebanon.
newsitem.headline: World Bank sharply increases funding for Lebanon.

text.p: The World Bank has quadrupled its annual funding available to Lebanon and has allotted $420 million to it this year, World Bank President James Wolfensohn said.
The bank trusted the Lebanese government and was imposing no conditions on the increased funding, Wolfensohn told a news conference on Sunday evening during his first visit to Lebanon.

"In 1997 alone we have done $270 million at the bank (for Lebanon) and another $150 million from the IFC (International Finance Corporation). That's a total of $420 million, of which $100 million were guarantees," Wolfensohn said.
"Before that we were operating at the rate of about $100 million a year and we've increased that to a continual rate of over $400 million a year."
Wolfensohn said the World Bank had also increased emergency funding for Lebanon by $50 million to a total of $150 million of which some $75-80 million had already been spent.

The increased help follows a comment made by Wolfensohn during Israel's devastating 17-day blitz of Lebanon in April 1996 that the World Bank had not developed a strong enough programme to help Lebanon's postwar reconstruction and would now take the opportunity to do so.
"We very much trust the government (of Lebanon) and believe in what they are doing," Wolfensohn told Sunday's news conference.

"There is literally no holdback on the part of the bank. There are no conditions to be met. It's a question simply of making effective use of the money and we're working really very harmoniously with the government now and all sectors to try and spend the money," he added.

Listing World Bank and IFC funding for Lebanon, Wolfensohn said programmes totalling $600 million had already been approved, $1 billion pledged at a Friends of Lebanon donors conference in Washington last December was going to be approved and the IFC was providing another $150 million a year.
The amounts were "very, very, high" in comparison with the bank's contribution to other countries in the region, he said.
The funds were earmarked for social programmes including health and education, he said.
Spending of the first $600 million by Lebanon, which had been relatively slow to start, was now going to increase very rapidly, Wolfensohn added.
Lebanese Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri said the World Bank and IFC contributions for Lebanon would total $2.2 billion over the next four years.
